## TL;DR

Added read-only triage details for worktrees that `repoos gc` already retains. The dry-run report and Control page now show a protected class, recommended action, age, last commit date, and whether the branch is merged. Documented the classes and recommendations from the actual dry-run inventory in this worktree. The sweep still removes only items its existing safety checks prove disposable; this task added no unsafe removal path and removed no worktree or branch.

## Work and rationale

I began with the task’s requested evidence: read #1055 and traced `src/core/worktree-gc.ts`, the `gc` CLI command, the cached system worktree-GC endpoint, and the existing cleanup preview in `SystemResourcePanel.vue`. I ran `repoos gc --dry-run` before making changes. It reported no safe candidates, 14 retained managed worktrees, and 3 external worktrees. The retained reasons came from the real inventory: live task state, human ownership, ignored/local data, and branches whose task-file content was not represented in main. I used those reasons to define the triage classes instead of speculating about classes that were not present.

The core sweep now enriches each retained row with a `protectedClass`, `recommendedAction`, `ageDays`, `lastCommitDate`, and `branchMerged`. The class uses the reported retention reason, with a live task taking precedence over its dirty paths because the task’s live lifecycle is the decisive reason it must stay. Directory birth time supplies age where the platform exposes it; unreadable or vanished paths remain unknown. The branch’s latest commit timestamp and ancestry against main supply the remaining Git metadata.

The CLI prints these details in plain text and has a `--json` output branch for machine-readable reports. The existing system worktree cleanup preview displays the same triage fields for retained worktrees. I added a shot fixture example so the preview has representative retained metadata in captures. The design note records the observed counts and examples, recommends keeping live work, asking the human about human-owned/local/unmerged work, and fixing lifecycle-record failures before cleanup. External worktrees stay outside RepoOS’s inspection and management boundary.

I left removal of protected worktrees unimplemented. The task asks for only non-destructive work, and the current GC already leaves unsafe entries in place. A future destructive flow must be designed around per-worktree confirmation and preservation/restoration of the branch and dirty state before removal; merely changing the recommendation to archive does not preserve work. Scheduled cleanup continues to be limited to the existing safe case from #1004/#1055.

## Approaches tried

I first attempted `repoos gc --dry-run --json` while the installed CLI was still routing to an older build, and it emitted the existing text output. I then ran the task build’s entry point directly with Bun. That produced a JSON report containing the new class, recommendation, age, last commit date, and merged fields for each retained row. This confirmed the implementation while also exposing that the installed executable can lag the task worktree build.

For the UI, I reused the existing Control page cleanup preview rather than creating a new Worktrees screen. That preview already displays the exact retained records from the same GC report, so adding triage facts there keeps the interface and CLI aligned without expanding product scope.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped check found formatting issues in the three edited source files. I ran `bun run fmt` and repeated the required check. Remote validation hosts could not pass their throughput probes, so RepoOS queued the serialized local fallback. The fallback completed successfully: formatting, lint, build, rendered contrast, changed-path tests, and UI smoke all passed.

The check workflow created WIP checkpoint commits itself before validation. I did not run `git add` or `git commit` directly. No unsafe worktree or branch was removed. I also did not add a preservation-backed deletion feature, since that would cross the task’s non-destructive implementation boundary and needs a separate reviewed design and restore test.

## Key learnings

The current retained population is heterogeneous: “protected” is not one lifecycle state. Live tasks, human-owned tasks, local data, unmerged contributions, and unknown lifecycle records need different follow-up. The exact reason and the structured dirty/source-path evidence should remain available alongside the recommendation; a recommendation alone is not enough to decide whether work can be archived.

Age is an operational hint, not proof that work is disposable. Likewise, a task marked done or archived does not establish that its branch content is safely present in main. The existing GC’s content proof remains the authority for automatic removal, and this triage metadata must not become a shortcut around it.

The Control page’s cleanup preview is already the shared human-facing report surface. Adding class and action there is a smaller and more consistent change than building a second worktree inventory UI. Finally, CLI JSON support should be verified against the exact build being exercised; a stale installed executable can make source changes appear absent even after code compiles.
